title: Schedule FA for RSU Holders: How to Fill Table A2 and Table A3 in ITR-2
summary: How to disclose vested RSUs in Schedule FA of ITR-2: who files, Table A2 and A3 column by column, the SBI TTBR date for each value and a filled example.
body_markdown:
If your RSUs from a foreign employer have vested, you declare the shares in Schedule FA of your income tax return every year you hold them. This applies whether or not you sold any shares, received a dividend or made a gain.


Schedule FA is a disclosure schedule, so filling it in does not add to your tax. Leaving it out or filling it in wrongly carries its own penalty, which has nothing to do with how much tax you owe.


This guide walks through the schedule in six steps, column by column, with one example carried into a filled Table A3. For the rest of the return, including Schedule S, Schedule CG and the foreign tax credit, start with the[ITR guide for RSU holders](https://paasa.com/blog/itr-for-rsu-holders) .


## Table of contents

## What Schedule FA asks from an RSU holder


Schedule FA (Foreign Assets) is a section of ITR-2 and ITR-3 where you list every foreign asset you held at any time during the year. ITR-1 and ITR-4 do not have this schedule, which is one reason an RSU holder cannot use them.


For an RSU holder, the foreign assets are the vested shares and the overseas account that holds them. The schedule asks what you held, when you got it and what it was worth at three points. It does not compute any tax.


Schedule FA follows the calendar year, while the rest of your return follows the financial year. The return for AY 2026-27 (FY 2025-26) covers foreign assets held between 1 January 2025 and 31 December 2025.


Shares held at any time during Go in the return for


1 January 2025 to 31 December 2025 AY 2026-27 (FY 2025-26)


1 January 2026 to 31 December 2026 Tax Year 2026-27, filed in 2027


So shares that vested in February 2025 belong in the AY 2026-27 return, even though February 2025 falls in the previous financial year. Shares that vested in January 2026 wait for the next return, although the salary tax on them belongs to FY 2025-26.


This guide follows the[ITR-2 form notified for AY 2026-27](https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/sites/default/files/2026-04/Notification%20No.46_2026.pdf) . The forms for Tax Year 2026-27, the first year under the Income-tax Act, 2025, will set the Schedule FA format for returns filed in 2027.


## How do I complete Schedule FA in my ITR 2?


You complete Schedule FA in six steps. Confirm that you have to file it, list the RSU shares that qualify, pick the right tables, convert each value at the right SBI rate, and then fill Table A2 and Table A3.


### 1. Check whether you have to file it


You fill Schedule FA only if both of these are true:


- You are resident and ordinarily resident (ROR) in India for the year.
- You held a foreign asset, such as vested shares of a foreign company, at any time during the calendar year.


Non-residents and residents who are not ordinarily resident (RNOR) do not fill Schedule FA, even if they hold foreign shares. If you have moved to or from India recently, check your status with[resident vs RNOR vs non-resident](https://paasa.com/blog/resident-vs-rnor-vs-nonresident-india) before you go further.


It makes no difference whether you sold, whether the price rose or fell, or whether your employer already deducted TDS when the shares vested. TDS settles the tax on the perquisite, while Schedule FA is a separate disclosure.


### 2. List the RSU shares that qualify


Only vested shares count. Go through the calendar year and list every lot of shares that was yours on any day of it.


Status of the RSUs Reported in Schedule FA? Why


Unvested units No They are a promise of future shares, so you do not own a foreign asset yet


Vested shares you still hold Yes They are shares of a foreign company in your name


Shares sold during the calendar year Yes You held them for part of the year


Shares delivered to you and then sold to cover tax Yes They reached your account before the sale, so you held them during the year


Shares your employer withheld before delivery No They never reached your account, so you did not hold them


Shares from earlier years that you still hold Yes They are reported every year, up to and including the calendar year in which you sell the last of them


Shares bought through an employee stock purchase plan follow the same logic from the purchase date. See[how ESPP shares are taxed in India](https://paasa.com/blog/espp-tax-india) for that side.


### 3. Use Table A2 for the account and Table A3 for the shares


RSU holders need two tables in Part A of the schedule, and both are required.


Table What it is called in the form What you report there


A2 Details of Foreign Custodial Accounts The plan or brokerage account that holds your shares, one line per account


A3 Details of Foreign Equity and Debt Interest The shares themselves, one line per vest


The account your employer's plan administrator opens for you abroad is a foreign custodial account, so it belongs in Table A2. A return that lists the shares in A3 but leaves the account out of A2 is still incomplete.


If your vested shares sit in more than one overseas account, each account gets its own line in A2.


### 4. Convert every value at the SBI TTBR


Every figure in Schedule FA is in rupees. The conversion rate is the State Bank of India's telegraphic transfer buying rate (TTBR), and the date of the rate depends on the column you are filling.


Column What the value is SBI TTBR to use


Initial value of the investment Shares in the vest × FMV per share on the vest date Rate on the vest date


Peak value of investment during the period Highest value of the shares from the vest while you held them in the year Rate on the date of that peak


Closing value Shares from the vest still held on 31 December × closing price that day Rate on 31 December


Peak balance of the account (Table A2) Highest balance in the account during the year Rate on the date of that peak


Closing balance of the account (Table A2) Balance in the account on 31 December Rate on 31 December


Gross amounts paid or credited and gross sale proceeds (Tables A2 and A3) Dividends, interest and sale proceeds during the year Rate on 31 December


These dates come from the tax department's[step-by-step guide to Schedule FA](https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/sites/default/files/2026-03/Step%20by%20Step%20Guide%20FA%20FSI.pdf) . It says that peak balances, values of investment and amounts of foreign-sourced income are converted at the TTBR on the date of the peak balance, the date of investment or the closing date of the calendar year, which is 31 December.


They are different from the rate used elsewhere in your return. The perquisite in your Form 16 is converted at the TTBR of the last day of the month before the vest, so the initial value in Schedule FA will usually be a little different from the perquisite value. That gap is expected and is not an error.


The instructions do not say what to do when a date falls on a weekend or bank holiday. The common practice is to use the rate of the working day just before it. For where to find the rate, read[SBI TTBR explained](https://paasa.com/blog/sbi-ttbr-rate-explained) .


### 5. Fill Table A2 for the account


Table A2 has one line for each overseas account, and its columns are about the account, not the individual shares.


Column in Table A2 What to enter


Country name and code The country where the account is held


Name of financial institution The broker or plan administrator that holds the account


Address and ZIP code That institution's address, from your account statement


Account number The account number on your statement


Status Your ownership status; if you are both the legal and the beneficial owner, report yourself as the legal owner


Account opening date The date the account was opened


Peak balance during the period The highest balance in the account during the calendar year, in rupees


Closing balance The balance on 31 December, in rupees


Gross amount paid/credited to the account during the period Amounts credited to the account in the year, with the nature picked as interest, dividend, proceeds from sale or redemption, or other income


Enter amounts gross and convert them at the 31 December rate. A dividend goes in before the US tax withheld on it, not as the net amount that reached the account.


### 6. Fill Table A3 for the shares


Table A3 is where the vested shares go. Enter each vest as its own line, because each one has a different acquisition date and a different initial value.


Column in Table A3 What to enter for an RSU vest


Country name and code The country of the company whose shares you hold


Name of entity The company whose shares vested, which is the listed parent and not your Indian employer


Address and ZIP code The company's registered address


Nature of entity The type of entity, which is a company


Date of acquiring the interest The vest date


Initial value of the investment Shares in the vest × FMV on the vest date × TTBR on the vest date


Peak value of investment during the period The highest value of those shares in the calendar year


Closing value The value of the shares still held on 31 December


Total gross amount paid/credited with respect to the holding during the period Gross dividends received on those shares in the calendar year


Total gross proceeds from sale or redemption of investment during the period Gross sale proceeds if you sold any of those shares in the calendar year


The initial value of a vest stays the same in every year's return, since it is fixed on the vest date. The peak and closing values are worked out afresh for each calendar year.


The last two columns are the only place where income shows up in Schedule FA, and they are for disclosure alone. Like the gross amounts in Table A2, they are converted at the 31 December rate.


The tax on that income is computed elsewhere in the return, on financial year figures and at the month-end exchange rates that the tax rules prescribe. Dividends go under income from other sources and in Schedule FSI, and sales go in Schedule CG, so the amounts will not match Schedule FA rupee for rupee. See[how dividends on RSU shares are taxed](https://paasa.com/blog/dividend-income-from-rsu-shares-taxed) and[capital gains tax on RSU shares](https://paasa.com/blog/capital-gains-tax-rsu-shares) .


## Example: two vests in one calendar year


**Example.** Suppose you are a product manager in Hyderabad, resident and ordinarily resident, with RSUs in your US-listed employer. In 2025, 25 shares vest on 10 June at an FMV of $167 and another 25 vest on 10 December at an FMV of $314. Your employer recovers the TDS through payroll, so all 50 shares reach your account and you hold them through 31 December 2025.


The share price peaks at $328 on 17 December and closes the year at $314, and the company pays no dividend during the year.


Take the SBI TTBR as ₹85.30 on 10 June, ₹89.55 on 10 December, ₹89.50 on 17 December and ₹89.47 on 31 December 2025. These rates are illustrative and close to where the TTBR stood on those dates.


Column in Table A3 Line 1 (June vest) Line 2 (December vest)


Country name United States of America United States of America


Name of entity Your employer's listed parent company Your employer's listed parent company


Date of acquiring the interest 10 June 2025 10 December 2025


Initial value of the investment ₹3,56,128 (25 × $167 × ₹85.30) ₹7,02,968 (25 × $314 × ₹89.55)


Peak value of investment during the period ₹7,33,900 (25 × $328 × ₹89.50) ₹7,33,900 (25 × $328 × ₹89.50)


Closing value ₹7,02,340 (25 × $314 × ₹89.47) ₹7,02,340 (25 × $314 × ₹89.47)


Total gross amount paid/credited with respect to the holding Nil Nil


Total gross proceeds from sale or redemption Nil Nil


**Closing value of both lines together** **₹14,04,680**


### The result: two lines in Table A3, one for each vest date


Each line carries its own acquisition date and initial value, even though both lots are shares of the same company in the same account. The peak and closing values happen to match because both lots hold 25 shares.


The account that holds the 50 shares goes in Table A2 as one line. In the next return, which covers calendar year 2026, both lines appear again with the same initial values and fresh peak and closing values.


## Shares you sold, sell-to-cover shares and unvested units


Three situations cause most of the doubt, and each has a short rule.


- **Shares sold during the year.** Report the vest as usual, show only the shares still held on 31 December in the closing value (nil if you sold them all), and enter the sale amount under gross proceeds from sale.
- **Shares sold to cover tax.** Table A3 covers foreign equity held at any time during the calendar year. If your statement shows the shares were delivered to you and then sold to cover tax, you held them, so include them in the initial value of that vest and show what they sold for under gross proceeds from sale. If your employer withheld the shares before delivery, there is nothing to report for those shares, and the line for that vest covers only the shares delivered to you.
- **Unvested units.** Leave them out, because they become a foreign asset only on the date they vest.


A lot that you sold completely drops out of Schedule FA from the following calendar year. The gain or loss on any sale, including a sell-to-cover sale, is reported separately in Schedule CG.


## Documents to gather before you start


Nothing is uploaded with Schedule FA, but every figure in it comes from a statement. Collect these for the calendar year before you open the form:


- **Vesting confirmations:** the vest date, the number of shares and the FMV per share for every vest, including vests from earlier years that you still hold.
- **Brokerage or plan account statements:** shares held, sales, cash balances and the account number and opening date for Table A2.
- **Your employer's annual equity or stock plan report:** a summary of grants, vests, shares withheld for tax and shares delivered.
- **Dividend statements:** gross dividends and the tax withheld abroad, which you also need for the foreign tax credit.
- **Share prices and SBI TTBR:** the closing price on 31 December, the highest price in the year, and the TTBR for each date you use.


Form 16 and Form 12BA show the perquisite your employer taxed, but they do not have the vest-date rate or the peak and closing values. If your records are scattered,[how to keep records for RSU tax calculations](https://paasa.com/blog/how-to-keep-records-for-rsu-tax-calculations) shows what to save at each vest.


## Common mistakes RSU holders make in Schedule FA


- **Using the financial year.** Schedule FA covers 1 January to 31 December, so a vest in January to March belongs in the next year's return.
- **Reporting one combined line.** Each vest is a separate line in Table A3 with its own date and initial value, not one total for the whole holding.
- **Filling A3 and skipping A2.** The account that holds the shares has to be reported in Table A2 as well.
- **Copying the Form 16 perquisite as the initial value.** Form 16 uses the previous month-end rate, while Schedule FA uses the vest-date rate.
- **Assuming Form 16 covers it.** Salary tax on the perquisite does not disclose the asset, and you still have to file ITR-2 or ITR-3 with Schedule FA.
- **Leaving out shares you sold.** Shares held for even part of the calendar year are reported, with the sale proceeds shown.
- **Reporting only the first year.** The shares go in every year you hold them, not just the year they vested.


## What is the penalty for not reporting RSUs in Schedule FA?


The penalty is ₹10 lakh for each year in which a foreign asset is left out or reported inaccurately. It is levied under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015.


The penalty does not depend on unpaid tax. You can have paid every rupee due on your RSUs through payroll and still face it for leaving the shares out of the schedule.


Since 1 October 2024, the penalty is not levied where the total value of your foreign assets, other than immovable property, is ₹20 lakh or less. This relief covers the penalty alone, so you still report the shares in Schedule FA whatever they are worth.


The department receives data on overseas accounts from other countries under FATCA and the Common Reporting Standard, so an unreported plan account is likely to be noticed.


## If you missed Schedule FA in earlier years


The fix depends on the year and on whether any income was left out along with the shares.


- **FY 2025-26:** you can file a revised return until 31 March 2027 and add the schedule.
- **Earlier years where income was also missed:** an updated return (ITR-U) can be filed within 48 months of the end of the assessment year, with Schedule FA included in it.
- **Earlier years where only the Schedule FA entry is missing:** ITR-U usually cannot be used, because it is meant for reporting extra income.


RSU shares are taxed as salary when they vest, so most RSU holders who skipped Schedule FA fall in the third group. For them the options are the ₹20 lakh relief, where it applies, or FAST-DS 2026.


FAST-DS is a one-time disclosure scheme introduced by the Finance Act, 2026, and declarations can be filed until 31 December 2026. Foreign assets that were already taxed but never reported in Schedule FA can be declared for a flat fee of ₹1 lakh, as long as their total value does not exceed ₹5 crore. A valid declaration gives immunity from penalty and prosecution under the Black Money Act for what you declare.


For a year-by-year method, read[how to fix missed Schedule FA years](https://paasa.com/blog/fix-missed-schedule-fa-years) . The scheme itself is covered in[FAST-DS 2026 explained](https://paasa.com/blog/fast-ds-2026-explained) .
